answer:
Here is what I would raise at your check-up, most urgent first. Your records run up to mid-October 2026.

1. Your stool test (FIT) on 4 November 2025 was positive. Your records show no colonoscopy or other follow-up test since then. A positive stool test needs a colonoscopy to look at the bowel. Ask your doctor whether you still need one and how to book it. If you had it done somewhere else, it would not show in these records.

2. Your LDL ("bad") cholesterol was 131 mg/dL in February 2025, above the usual target of 99. Atorvastatin was prescribed two days later, and there is no cholesterol test on record since then. Ask whether you need a repeat lipid test to see how the statin is working.

3. Your last HbA1c (blood sugar average) was 6.9% in February 2026, about eight months ago, and no test is recorded since. People with diabetes usually have this every three to six months. Ask when your next one is due.

4. Your records show no urine albumin test, which checks for early kidney damage. Your eGFR (kidney filtration) was 69 in February 2026. People with type 2 diabetes usually need this urine test every year. Ask about it.

5. Your records show metformin ended in April 2024, and Jardiance was prescribed in February 2025. No diabetes medicine is listed in between, and your HbA1c rose from 7.4% to 8.3% over that time. This may be a gap in the records, but it is worth asking about.

6. No vaccines are recorded at all. Ask your doctor which ones you are due. For someone your age with diabetes this usually includes a shingles vaccine, a pneumonia vaccine, and a yearly flu shot.

Nothing is outstanding from the July 2025 chest scan: it showed no pulmonary embolism (blood clot in the lung), even though a blood test (D-dimer) was raised, and the chest wall pain that prompted it has resolved.
short: Positive stool test (Nov 2025) with no colonoscopy on record; LDL 131 with no cholesterol test since Feb 2025; last HbA1c Feb 2026; no urine albumin test; no vaccines recorded. Please check each of these.

items.says: The stool test (FIT) on 4 November 2025 was positive, and no colonoscopy or other follow-up test is recorded since.
items.why: A positive FIT needs a diagnostic colonoscopy. The only procedure in her records is a chest CT from July 2025.

absences.what: No colonoscopy or other follow-up bowel test after the positive stool test
absences.coverage: All her procedures in the pod, from the hospital records retrieved 2026-10-15. The only procedure is a chest CT from 2025-07-08. Records from other providers are not in the pod.

knowledge.says: A positive stool test is a screening signal, not a diagnosis. It needs a diagnostic colonoscopy to look for bowel cancer or polyps, usually soon after the result.
knowledge.guideline: USPSTF colorectal cancer screening recommendations; ACG and ASGE guidance on follow-up after a positive stool test.

items.says: LDL cholesterol was 131 mg/dL (high) in February 2025, and no cholesterol test is recorded since. Atorvastatin was prescribed just after that test.
items.why: On a statin, a repeat lipid panel is normally checked after starting and then periodically. The records show none after February 2025.

facts.says: Atorvastatin 20 mg tablet, take 1 tablet by mouth once daily
facts.name: Atorvastatin 20 mg tablet

absences.coverage: All 21 lab results in the pod, dated 2023 to 2026, from the hospital records retrieved 2026-10-15.

knowledge.says: A lipid panel is usually repeated about 4 to 12 weeks after a statin is started, then at intervals your doctor sets. The February 2025 result was taken before the statin was prescribed, so it is a baseline and not a check on the statin.
knowledge.guideline: ACC/AHA 2018 cholesterol management guideline; ADA Standards of Care for diabetes (statin therapy and lipid monitoring).

items.says: Your last HbA1c was 6.9% on 16 February 2026, about eight months before today, and no HbA1c is recorded since.
items.why: People with diabetes usually have HbA1c every three to six months, depending on whether their sugar is at target and whether treatment has changed.

absences.coverage: All HbA1c results in the pod, from the hospital records retrieved 2026-10-15.

knowledge.says: The usual schedule is every three months if sugar control is not at target or treatment has changed, and every six months if it is stable at target.
knowledge.guideline: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, glycemic monitoring.

items.says: No urine albumin-to-creatinine test is on record. Your eGFR was 69 in February 2026, and this urine test is the usual check for early kidney damage in type 2 diabetes.
items.why: Kidney damage in diabetes can be present before the eGFR changes, so the urine test is needed alongside eGFR each year.

absences.what: No urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) test on record
absences.coverage: All 21 lab results in the pod, dated 2023 to 2026, from the hospital records retrieved 2026-10-15. The test name is not in the pod.

knowledge.says: People with type 2 diabetes usually need a yearly urine albumin test and an eGFR to screen for kidney disease. Her eGFR is in the normal-to-mildly-reduced range, so the urine result matters.
knowledge.guideline: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, chronic kidney disease screening; KDIGO CKD guideline.

items.says: Metformin ended in April 2024 and Jardiance was prescribed in February 2025, with no diabetes medicine listed in between. Her HbA1c rose from 7.4% to 8.3% over that period.
items.why: This may be a gap in the records, but it is worth checking that she was on treatment during that time.

items.why: Her records contain no immunization entries, so any vaccines she has had are either missing from the records or were given elsewhere.

knowledge.says: Adults with diabetes are advised to have a yearly flu shot, a pneumococcal vaccine (she is over 65), and a recombinant shingles vaccine (over 50), plus COVID-19 and hepatitis B vaccines as current guidance advises.
knowledge.guideline: CDC adult immunization schedule; ADA Standards of Care (immunization section).

items.says: The July 2025 chest CT showed no pulmonary embolism, despite a raised D-dimer blood test, and the chest pain that prompted the scan has resolved. Nothing is outstanding from this.
items.why: A raised D-dimer does not confirm a clot on its own; the CT angiogram is the test that rules it in or out, and it was clear.

facts.says: CT angiography chest (pulmonary embolism protocol). Conclusion: No pulmonary embolism. Lungs are clear.
facts.name: CT angiography chest (pulmonary embolism protocol)
facts.quote: No pulmonary embolism. Lungs are clear.

knowledge.says: A raised D-dimer is non-specific and often rises for reasons other than a clot. A negative CT angiogram rules out pulmonary embolism.

links.says: The CT angiogram is the definitive test; the raised D-dimer was a screening result that the scan explained.
The LDL result was taken two days before atorvastatin was prescribed, so it is a pre-treatment value.
